text: Percy Bysshe Shelley (/bɪʃ/ ⓘ BISH;[1][2] 4 August 1792 – 8 July 1822) was an English writer regarded as one of the major English Romantic poets.[3][4] A radical in both his poetry and personal beliefs, Shelley did not achieve fame during his lifetime, but posthumous recognition of his poetic achievements grew steadily, influencing later poets such as Robert Browning, Algernon Charles Swinburne, Thomas Hardy, and W. B. Yeats. American literary critic Harold Bloom described him as "a superb craftsman, a lyric poet without rival, and surely one of the most advanced sceptical intellects ever to write a poem."[5] His reputation fluctuated in the 20th century but since the 1960s, he has gained increasing critical acclaim for the dynamic imagery in his poetry, his mastery of genres and verse forms, and the complex interplay of sceptical, idealist, and materialist ideas.[6][7] Among his best-known works are "Ozymandias" (1818), "Ode to the West Wind" (1819), "To a Skylark" (1820), "Adonais" (1821), the philosophical essay "The Necessity of Atheism" (1811), which may have been co-authored with his friend T. J. Hogg, and the political ballad "The Mask of Anarchy" (1819). His major works also include the verse dramas The Cenci (1819), Prometheus Unbound (1820), and Hellas (1822), and the long narrative poems Alastor, or The Spirit of Solitude (1815), Julian and Maddalo (1819), and The Triumph of Life (1822). Shelley also wrote prose fiction and essays on political, social, and philosophical topics, much of which was not published during his lifetime or only appeared in expurgated form due to the risk of prosecution for political and religious libel.[8] From the 1820s, his works became popular in Owenist, Chartist, and radical political circles,[9] and later attracted admirers such as Karl Marx, Mahatma Gandhi, and George Bernard Shaw.[9][10][11] His life was marked by family crises, ill health, and opposition to his atheism, political views, and defiance of social norms. He went into permanent self-exile in Italy in 1818 and over the next four years produced what Zachary Leader and Michael O'Neill call "some of the finest poetry of the Romantic period".[12] His second wife, Mary Shelley, was the author of Frankenstein. He died in a boating accident in 1822 at age 29. Shelley was born on 4 August 1792 at Field Place, Warnham, Sussex, England.[13][14] He was the eldest son of Sir Timothy Shelley, 2nd Baronet of Castle Goring, a Whig Member of Parliament for Horsham from 1790 to 1792 and for Shoreham between 1806 and 1812, and his wife, Elizabeth Pilfold, daughter of a successful butcher.[15] He had four younger sisters and one much younger brother. His early childhood was sheltered and mostly happy, with strong bonds to his sisters and mother, who encouraged him to hunt, fish, and ride.[16][17] At age six, he attended a day school run by the vicar of Warnham church, where he showed an impressive memory and talent for languages.[18] In 1802, he entered the Syon House Academy of Brentford, Middlesex, where his cousin Thomas Medwin was a student. Shelley was bullied and unhappy at the school and sometimes responded with violent rage. He also began experiencing nightmares, hallucinations, and sleepwalking that would recur throughout his life. He developed an interest in science, which complemented his reading of mystery, romance, and supernatural tales. During holidays at Field Place, his sisters were often frightened by his experiments with gunpowder, acids, and electricity. Back at school, he blew up a paling fence with gunpowder.[19][20] In 1804, Shelley entered Eton College, which he later recalled with loathing. He faced severe mob bullying, referred to as "Shelley-baits," attributed to his aloofness, nonconformity, and refusal to participate in fagging. His peculiarities and violent outbursts earned him the nickname "Mad Shelley." His interest in the occult and science continued, with contemporaries reporting he gave an electric shock to a master, blew up a tree stump with gunpowder, and attempted to raise spirits through occult rituals.[24] In his final year at Eton, he was influenced by part-time teacher James Lind, who encouraged his interest in the occult and introduced him to liberal and radical authors. Shelley also developed an interest in Plato and idealist philosophy, which he pursued through self-study.[25][26] According to Richard Holmes, by the end of his time at Eton, Shelley had gained a reputation as a classical scholar and a tolerated eccentric.[25] In his last term, his first novel, Zastrozzi, was published and he gained a following among his peers.[25] Before enrolling at University College, Oxford, in October 1810, Shelley completed Original Poetry by Victor and Cazire (written with his sister Elizabeth), the verse melodrama The Wandering Jew, and the gothic novel St. Irvine; or, The Rosicrucian: A Romance (published 1811).[27][28] At Oxford, Shelley attended few lectures and spent long hours reading and conducting scientific experiments in a laboratory he set up in his room.[29] He met fellow student Thomas Jefferson Hogg, who became his closest friend. Under Hogg's influence, Shelley became increasingly politicized, developing strong radical and anti-Christian views. These views were dangerous in the context of Britain's war with Napoleonic France, and Shelley's father warned him against Hogg's influence.[30] In the winter of 1810–1811, Shelley published a series of anonymous political poems and tracts: Posthumous Fragments of Margaret Nicholson, The Necessity of Atheism (written in collaboration with Hogg), and A Poetical Essay on the Existing State of Things. He mailed The Necessity of Atheism to all bishops and heads of colleges at Oxford and was called before the college's fellows, including Dean George Rowley. His refusal to answer questions about authorship led to his expulsion from Oxford on 25 March 1811, along with Hogg. Upon hearing of his son's expulsion, Shelley's father threatened to cut off all contact with him unless he returned home and studied under tutors appointed by him. Shelley's refusal resulted in a falling-out with his father.[31] In late December 1810, Shelley met Harriet Westbrook, a pupil at the same boarding school as his sisters. They corresponded frequently during that winter and after Shelley's expulsion from Oxford.[32] Shelley shared his radical views on politics, religion, and marriage with Harriet, and they gradually convinced each other that she was oppressed by her father and at school.[33] Shelley's infatuation with Harriet developed in the months following his expulsion, during a period of severe emotional strain caused by family conflict, the breakdown of his romance with his cousin Harriet Grove, and his unfounded belief that he might have a fatal illness.[34] At the same time, Harriet's elder sister Eliza encouraged the young girl's romance with Shelley.[35] Shelley's correspondence with Harriet intensified in July while holidaying in Wales, and in response to her urgent pleas for protection, he returned to London in early August. Putting aside his philosophical objections to marriage, he left with the 16-year-old Harriet for Edinburgh, Scotland, on 25 August 1811, and they were married there on 28 August.[36] Upon hearing of the elopement, Harriet's father, John Westbrook, and Shelley's father, Timothy, cut off the allowances of the bride and groom. (Shelley's father believed his son had married beneath him, as Harriet's father had earned his fortune in trade and owned a tavern and coffee house.)[37] Surviving on borrowed money, Shelley and Harriet stayed in Edinburgh for a month, with Hogg living under the same roof. The trio then moved to York in October, and Shelley went to Sussex to settle matters with his father, leaving Harriet behind with Hogg. Upon returning from his unsuccessful trip, Shelley found that Eliza had moved in with Harriet and Hogg. Harriet confessed that Hogg had tried to seduce her while Shelley was away. Shelley, Harriet, and Eliza soon left for Keswick in the Lake District, leaving Hogg in York.[38] From June 1811, Shelley was also involved in an intense platonic relationship with Elizabeth Hitchener, a 28-year-old unmarried schoolteacher with whom he corresponded frequently. Hitchener became his confidante and intellectual companion as he developed his views on politics, religion, ethics, and personal relationships.[39] Shelley became increasingly radicalized as the war with Napoleon brought economic recession, food riots, and government suppression of political dissent.[40] He proposed that Hitchener join him, Harriet, and Eliza in a communal household where all property would be shared.[41] The Shelleys and Eliza spent December and January in Keswick, where Shelley visited Robert Southey, whose poetry he admired. Southey was impressed with Shelley, despite their political differences, and predicted great things for him as a poet. Southey also informed Shelley that William Godwin, author of Political Justice, which had greatly influenced him in his youth and which Shelley admired, was still alive. Shelley wrote to Godwin, offering himself as his devoted disciple. Godwin, who had modified many of his earlier radical views, advised Shelley to reconcile with his father, become a scholar before publishing, and abandon his plans for political agitation in Ireland.[42] Meanwhile, Shelley met his father's patron, Charles Howard, 11th Duke of Norfolk, who helped secure the reinstatement of Shelley's allowance.[43] With Harriet's allowance also restored, Shelley had the funds for his Irish venture. Their departure for Ireland was prompted by increasing hostility from their landlord and neighbors, alarmed by Shelley's scientific experiments, pistol shooting, and radical political views. As tensions grew, Shelley claimed he had been attacked in his home by ruffians, an event that may have been real or a delusional episode triggered by stress. This was the first of a series of episodes in which Shelley claimed to have been attacked by strangers during personal crises.[44] Early in 1812, Shelley wrote, published, and personally distributed in Dublin two political tracts: An Address, to the Irish People; and Proposals for an Association of Philanthropists. He also delivered a speech at a meeting of Daniel O'Connell's Catholic Committee, calling for Catholic emancipation, repeal of the Acts of Union, and an end to the oppression of the Irish poor while cautioning against violence.[45] Reports of Shelley's subversive activities were sent to the Home Secretary.[46] Returning from Ireland, the Shelley household traveled to Wales, then to the small coastal village of Lynmouth in Devon. There they were joined by Hitchener, and again came under government surveillance for distributing subversive literature. After several months, Hitchener had a falling out with the Shelleys and left. When Shelley's 15-year-old Irish servant was arrested for distributing Shelley's Declaration of Rights and his ballad attacking the government, The Devil's Walk, Shelley and his companions fled.[47][a] In September 1812, the Shelley household settled in Tremadog, Wales, where Shelley worked on Queen Mab, a utopian allegory with extensive notes promoting atheism, free love, republicanism, and vegetarianism. The poem was published the following year in a private edition of 250 copies, though few were initially distributed due to the risk of prosecution for seditious and religious libel.[49] In February 1813, Shelley claimed he was attacked in his home at night. The incident may have been real, a hallucination caused by stress, or a hoax staged to escape government surveillance, creditors, and local political entanglements. The Shelleys and Eliza fled to Ireland, then to London.[50] Back in England, Shelley's debts grew as he tried unsuccessfully to reach a financial settlement with his father. On 23 June, Harriet gave birth to a girl, Eliza Ianthe Shelley (known as Ianthe), and in the following months the relationship between Shelley and his wife deteriorated. Shelley resented the influence Harriet's sister had over her, while Harriet became alienated from Shelley due to his close friendship with an attractive widow, Mrs. Harriet de Boinville.[51] Mrs. Boinville had married a French revolutionary émigré and hosted a salon where Shelley discussed politics, philosophy, and vegetarianism.[52][53] She became a confidante during Shelley's marital crisis.[54] During a breakdown, Shelley moved into Mrs. Boinville's home outside London. In February and March 1814, he became infatuated with her married daughter, Cornelia Turner, aged 18, and wrote erotic poetry about her in his notebook.[55][56] Following Ianthe's birth, the Shelleys moved frequently across London, Wales, the Lake District, Scotland, and Berkshire to escape creditors and find a home.[57] In March 1814, Shelley remarried Harriet in London to settle any doubts about the legality of their Edinburgh wedding and secure the rights of their child. Nevertheless, the Shelleys lived apart for most of the following months, and Shelley reflected bitterly on "my rash & heartless union with Harriet".[58] In May 1814, Shelley began visiting his mentor, William Godwin, almost daily. He soon fell in love with Godwin's sixteen-year-old daughter, Mary, whose mother was the late feminist writer Mary Wollstonecraft. Shelley and Mary declared their love for each other during a visit to her mother's grave in the churchyard of St Pancras Old Church on 26 June. When Shelley told Godwin he intended to leave Harriet and live with Mary, his mentor banished him from the house and forbade Mary from seeing him. Shelley and Mary eloped to Europe on 28 July, taking Mary's step-sister Claire Clairmont with them. Before leaving, Shelley had secured a loan of £3,000 but had left most of the funds at the disposal of Godwin and Harriet, who was again pregnant. The financial arrangement with Godwin led to rumors that he had sold his daughters to Shelley.[60] Shelley, Mary, and Claire traveled across war-ravaged France, where Shelley wrote to Harriet, asking her to meet them in Switzerland with the money he had left for her. Hearing nothing from Harriet in Switzerland and unable to secure sufficient funds or suitable accommodation, the three traveled to Germany and Holland, before returning to England on 13 September.[61] Shelley spent the next few months trying to raise loans and avoid bailiffs. Mary was pregnant, lonely, depressed, and ill. Her mood worsened when she learned that on 30 November, Harriet had given birth to Charles Bysshe Shelley, heir to the Shelley fortune and baronetcy.[62] This was followed, in early January 1815, by news that Shelley's grandfather, Sir Bysshe, had died, leaving an estate worth £220,000. The settlement of the estate and a financial settlement between Shelley and his father (now Sir Timothy) were not finalized until April the following year.[63] In February 1815, Mary gave premature birth to a baby girl who died ten days later, deepening her depression. In the following weeks, Mary became close to Hogg, who temporarily moved into the household. Shelley was almost certainly having a sexual relationship with Claire at this time, and it is possible that Mary, with Shelley's encouragement, was also having a sexual relationship with Hogg. In May, Claire left the household at Mary's insistence to reside in Lynmouth.[64] In August, Shelley and Mary moved to Bishopsgate, where Shelley worked on Alastor, a long poem in blank verse based on the myth of Narcissus and Echo. Alastor was published in an edition of 250 copies in early 1816 to poor sales and largely unfavourable reviews from the conservative press.[65][66] On 24 January 1816, Mary gave birth to William Shelley. Shelley was delighted to have another son, but was suffering from the strain of prolonged financial negotiations with his father, Harriet, and William Godwin. Shelley showed signs of delusional behavior and was contemplating an escape to the continent.[67] Claire initiated a sexual relationship with Lord Byron in April 1816, just before his self-exile on the continent, and then arranged for Byron to meet Shelley, Mary, and her in Geneva.[68] Shelley admired Byron's poetry and had sent him Queen Mab and other poems. Shelley's party arrived in Geneva in May and rented a house close to Villa Diodati, on the shores of Lake Geneva, where Byron was staying. There Shelley, Byron, and the others engaged in discussions about literature, science, and "various philosophical doctrines". One night, while Byron was reciting Coleridge's Christabel, Shelley suffered a severe panic attack with hallucinations. The previous night Mary had had a more productive vision or nightmare which inspired her novel Frankenstein.[69] Shelley and Byron then took a boating tour around Lake Geneva, which inspired Shelley to write his "Hymn to Intellectual Beauty", his first substantial poem since Alastor.[70] A tour of

Shelley was delighted to have another son but was suffering from the strain of prolonged financial negotiations with his father, Harriet, and William Godwin, showing signs of delusional behavior and contemplating an escape to the continent. Claire initiated a sexual relationship with Lord Byron in April 1816, just before his self-exile, and arranged for Byron to meet Shelley, Mary, and herself in Geneva. Shelley admired Byron's poetry and had previously sent him *Queen Mab* and other poems. Shelley's party arrived in Geneva in May and rented a house near Villa Diodati, where Byron was staying. There, Shelley, Byron, and the others engaged in discussions about literature, science, and "various philosophical doctrines." One night, while Byron recited Coleridge's *Christabel*, Shelley suffered a severe panic attack with hallucinations. The previous night, Mary had a more productive vision or nightmare that inspired her novel *Frankenstein*. Shelley and Byron took a boating tour around Lake Geneva, which inspired Shelley to write his "Hymn to Intellectual Beauty," his first substantial poem since *Alastor*. A tour of Chamonix inspired *Mont Blanc*, described as an atheistic response to Coleridge's "Hymn before Sunrise in the Vale of Chamoni." During this tour, Shelley often signed guest books declaring himself an atheist, which was seen by British tourists including Southey, hardening attitudes against him back home. Relations between Byron and Shelley's party became strained when Byron was told Claire was pregnant with his child. Shelley, Mary, and Claire left Switzerland in late August, with arrangements for the expected baby still unclear, though Shelley made provision for Claire and the baby in his will. In January 1817, Claire gave birth to a daughter by Byron, whom she named Alba and later renamed Allegra in accordance with Byron's wishes. Shelley and Mary returned to England in September 1816, and in early October heard that Mary's half-sister Fanny Imlay had killed herself. Godwin believed Fanny had been in love with Shelley, and Shelley suffered depression and guilt over her death, writing: "Friend had I known thy secret grief / Should we have parted so." Further tragedy followed in December when Shelley's estranged wife Harriet drowned herself in the Serpentine, pregnant and living alone, believing she had been abandoned. In her suicide letter, she asked Shelley to take custody of their son Charles but to leave their daughter in her sister Eliza's care. Shelley married Mary Godwin on 30 December, despite his philosophical objections to the institution, to help secure custody of his children by Harriet and to placate Godwin, who had refused to see them due to their previous adulterous relationship. After a prolonged legal battle, the Court of Chancery awarded custody of Shelley and Harriet's children to foster parents, citing Shelley's abandonment of his first wife without cause and his atheism. In March 1817, the Shelleys moved to Marlow, Buckinghamshire, where Shelley's friend Thomas Love Peacock lived. The household included Claire and her baby Allegra, both of whom Mary resented. Shelley's generosity with money and increasing debts caused financial and marital stress, as did Godwin's frequent requests for financial help. On 2 September, Mary gave birth to a daughter, Clara Everina Shelley. Soon after, Shelley left for London with Claire, increasing Mary's resentment toward her stepsister. Shelley was arrested for two days in London over money he owed, and attorneys visited Mary in Marlow over his debts. Shelley participated in the literary and political circle surrounding Leigh Hunt, meeting William Hazlitt and John Keats. His major work during this time was *Laon and Cythna*, a long narrative poem featuring incest and attacks on religion, which was hastily withdrawn due to fears of prosecution for religious libel and reissued as *The Revolt of Islam* in January 1818. He also published two political tracts under a pseudonym: *A Proposal for putting Reform to the Vote throughout the Kingdom* (March 1817) and *An Address to the People on the Death of Princess Charlotte* (November 1817). In December, he wrote "Ozymandias," considered one of his finest sonnets, as part of a competition with Horace Smith. On 12 March 1818, the Shelleys and Claire left England to escape its "tyranny civil and religious," with a doctor recommending Shelley go to Italy for his chronic lung complaint. Shelley arranged to take Claire's daughter, Allegra, to Byron in Venice. After traveling through France and Italy, Shelley left Mary and baby Clara at Bagni di Lucca while traveling with Claire to Venice to see Byron and arrange for Allegra's visit. Byron invited the Shelleys to stay at his summer residence in Este, and Shelley urged Mary to meet him there. Clara became seriously ill on the journey and died on 24 September in Venice. Following Clara's death, Mary fell into a long period of depression and emotional estrangement from Shelley. On 1 December, the Shelleys moved to Naples, where they stayed for three months. During this period, Shelley was ill, depressed, and almost suicidal, reflected in his poem "Stanzas written in Dejection – December 1818, Near Naples." While in Naples, Shelley registered the birth and baptism of a baby girl, Elena Adelaide Shelley (born 27 December), naming himself as the father and falsely naming Mary as the mother. The parentage of Elena has never been conclusively established; biographers have speculated she was adopted to console Mary, Shelley's child by Claire, his child by his servant Elise Foggi, or the child of a "mysterious lady" who followed him to the continent. Shelley registered the birth and baptism on 27 February 1819, and the household left Naples for Rome the following day, leaving Elena with carers. Elena died in a poor suburb of Naples on 9 June 1820. In Rome, Shelley was in poor health, likely having developed nephritis and tuberculosis, which later went into remission. Nevertheless, he made significant progress on three major works: *Julian and Maddalo*, *Prometheus Unbound*, and *The Cenci*. *Julian and Maddalo* is an autobiographical poem exploring the relationship between Shelley and Byron and analyzing Shelley's personal crises of 1818 and 1819, completed in the summer of 1819 but not published in his lifetime. *Prometheus Unbound* is a long dramatic poem inspired by Aeschylus's retelling of the Prometheus myth, completed in late 1819 and published in 1820. *The Cenci* is a verse drama of rape, murder, and incest based on the story of the Renaissance Count Cenci and his daughter Beatrice, completed in September and published that year, becoming one of his most popular works and the only one to have two authorized editions in his lifetime. Shelley's three-year-old son William died in June 1819, probably of malaria, causing further decline in his health and deepening Mary's depression. On 4 August, Mary wrote: "We have now lived five years together; and if all the events of the five years were blotted out, I might be happy." The Shelleys were living in Livorno when, in September, Shelley heard of the Peterloo Massacre. Within two weeks, he completed *The Mask of Anarchy*, one of his most famous political poems, and sent it to Leigh Hunt for publication. Hunt refused to publish it due to fear of prosecution for seditious libel; it was officially published in 1832. In October, the Shelleys moved to Florence, where Shelley read a scathing review of *The Revolt of Islam* (and its earlier version *Laon and Cythna*) in the conservative *Quarterly Review*. He was angered by the personal attack on him, which he mistakenly believed was written by Southey, and this bitterness lasted for the rest of his life. On 12 November, Mary gave birth to a boy, Percy Florence Shelley. Around the time of Percy's birth, the Shelleys met Sophia Stacey, a ward of one of Shelley's uncles staying at the same pension. Sophia, a talented harpist and singer, formed a friendship with Shelley while Mary was preoccupied with her newborn son. Shelley wrote at least five love poems and fragments for Sophia, including "Song written for an Indian Air." The Shelleys moved to Pisa in January 1820, ostensibly to consult a doctor. There, they became friends with the Irish republican Margaret Mason (Lady Margaret Mountcashell) and her lover George William Tighe. Mrs. Mason became the inspiration for Shelley's poem "The Sensitive Plant," and his discussions with her and Tighe influenced his political thought and his interest in Thomas Malthus's population theories. In March, Shelley wrote to friends that Mary was depressed, suicidal, and hostile toward him. Shelley was also beset by financial worries as creditors from England pressed him for payment and he made secret payments related to his "Neapolitan charge" Elena. Meanwhile, Shelley was writing *A Philosophical View of Reform*, a political essay begun in Rome, which remained unpublished in his lifetime and is considered "one of the most advanced and sophisticated documents of political philosophy in the nineteenth century." Another crisis erupted in June when Shelley claimed he had been assaulted in the Pisan post office by a man accusing him of foul crimes. Biographer James Bieri suggests this incident may have been a delusional episode caused by extreme stress, as Shelley was being blackmailed by a former servant, Paolo Foggi, over baby Elena. It is likely the blackmail was connected to a story spread by another former servant, Elise Foggi, that Shelley had fathered a child by Claire in Naples and sent it to a foundling home. Shelley, Claire, and Mary denied the story, and Elise later recanted. In July, hearing that John Keats was seriously ill in England, Shelley wrote to invite him to stay with him in Pisa. Keats replied with hopes of seeing him, but arrangements were made for Keats to travel to Rome. Following Keats's death in 1821, Shelley wrote *Adonais*, considered by Harold Bloom one of the major pastoral elegies. The poem was published in Pisa in July 1821 but sold few copies. In early July 1820, Shelley heard that baby Elena had died on 9 June. In the months following the post office incident and Elena's death, relations between Mary and Claire deteriorated, and Claire spent most of the next two years living separately from the Shelleys, mainly in Florence. That December, Shelley met Teresa (Emilia) Viviani, the 19-year-old daughter of the Governor of Pisa living in a convent awaiting marriage. Shelley visited her several times and they began a passionate correspondence, which dwindled after her marriage in September. Emilia inspired Shelley's major poem *Epipsychidion*. In March 1821, Shelley completed "A Defence of Poetry," a response to Peacock's article "The Four Ages of Poetry," with its famous conclusion "Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world," remaining unpublished in his lifetime. Shelley went alone to Ravenna in early August to see Byron, making a detour to Livorno to meet Claire. He stayed with Byron for two weeks and invited him to spend the winter in Pisa. After hearing Byron recite his fifth canto of *Don Juan*, Shelley wrote to Mary: "I despair of rivalling Byron." In November, Byron moved into Villa Lanfranchi in Pisa, just across the river from the Shelleys, becoming the center of the "Pisan circle," which included Shelley, Thomas Medwin, Edward Williams, and Edward Trelawny. In the early months of 1822, Shelley became increasingly close to Jane Williams, who lived with her partner Edward Williams in the same building. Shelley wrote several love poems for Jane, including "The Serpent is shut out of Paradise" and "With a Guitar, to Jane," causing increasing tension among Shelley, Edward Williams, and Mary. Claire arrived in Pisa in April at Shelley's invitation, and soon after heard that her daughter Allegra had died of typhus in Ravenna. The Shelleys and Claire then moved to Villa Magni, near Lerici, on the shores of the Gulf of La Spezia. Shelley acted as mediator between Claire and Byron over arrangements for Allegra's burial, and the added strain led to Shelley having a series of hallucinations. Mary almost died from a miscarriage on 16 June, saved by Shelley's first aid. Two days later, Shelley wrote to a friend that there was no sympathy between Mary and him and that if the past and future could be obliterated, he would be content in his boat with Jane and her guitar. That same day, he wrote to Trelawny asking for prussic acid. The following week, Shelley woke the household with screaming over a nightmare or hallucination in which he saw Edward and Jane Williams as walking corpses and himself strangling Mary. During this time, Shelley was writing his final major poem, the unfinished *The Triumph of Life*, which Harold Bloom called "the most despairing poem he wrote." On 1 July 1822, Shelley and Edward Williams sailed in Shelley's new boat, the *Don Juan*, to Livorno to meet Leigh Hunt and Byron to arrange a new journal, *The Liberal*. After the meeting, on 8 July, Shelley, Williams, and their boat boy sailed out of Livorno for Lerici. A few hours later, the *Don Juan*, an open boat custom-built in Genoa, and its inexperienced crew were lost in a storm. Mary Shelley declared in her "Note on Poems of 1822" (1839) that the boat's design had a defect and was never seaworthy. The sinking was probably due to the severe storm and poor seamanship. Shelley's badly decomposed body washed ashore at Viareggio ten days later and was identified by Trelawny from clothing and a copy of Keats's *Lamia* in a jacket pocket. On 16 August, his body was cremated on a beach near Viareggio, and the ashes were buried in the Protestant Cemetery of Rome. The day after the news of his death reached England, the Tory London newspaper *The Courier* printed: "Shelley, the writer of some infidel poetry, has been drowned; now he knows whether there is God or no." Shelley's ashes were reburied in a different plot at the cemetery in 1823. His grave bears the Latin inscription *Cor Cordium* (Heart of Hearts) and a few lines of "Ariel's Song" from Shakespeare's *The Tempest*: "Nothing of him that doth fade / But doth suffer a sea change / Into something rich and strange." When Shelley's body was cremated, his presumed heart resisted burning and was retrieved by Trelawny. The heart may have been calcified from an earlier tubercular infection or could have been his liver. Trelawny gave the scorched organ to Hunt, who preserved it in spirits of wine and refused to hand it over to Mary. He eventually relented, and the heart was buried either in Rome or elsewhere.

On 16 August, Percy Bysshe Shelley's body was cremated on a beach near Viareggio, and his ashes were buried in the Protestant Cemetery of Rome. The day after the news of his death reached England, the Tory newspaper The Courier published: "Shelley, the writer of some infidel poetry, has been drowned; now he knows whether there is God or no." In 1823, Shelley's ashes were reburied in a different plot at the cemetery, where his grave bears the Latin inscription Cor Cordium (Heart of Hearts) and a few lines from "Ariel's Song" in Shakespeare's The Tempest: "Nothing of him that doth fade / But doth suffer a sea change / Into something rich and strange." During the cremation, his presumed heart resisted burning and was retrieved by Trelawny; it may have been calcified from a prior tubercular infection or could have been his liver. Trelawny gave the scorched organ to Hunt, who preserved it in spirits of wine and refused to hand it over to Mary Shelley; eventually, the heart was buried either at St Peter's Church, Bournemouth, or in Christchurch Priory. Hunt also retrieved a piece of Shelley's jawbone, which was given to the Shelley-Keats Memorial in Rome in 1913. Shelley's paternal grandfather was Bysshe Shelley (21 June 1731 – 6 January 1815), who was created Sir Bysshe Shelley, 1st Baronet of Castle Goring, in 1806; upon his death in 1815, Shelley's father inherited the baronetcy, becoming Sir Timothy Shelley. Shelley was the eldest of several legitimate children; Bieri suggests he had an older illegitimate brother, though little is known about him; his younger siblings were Elizabeth (1794–1831), Hellen (1796–1796), Mary (1797–1884), Hellen (1799–1885), Margaret (1801–1887), and John (1806–1866). He had two children with his first wife Harriet: Eliza Ianthe Shelley (1813–1876) and Charles Bysshe Shelley (1814–1826); four children with his second wife Mary: an unnamed daughter born in 1815 who died after ten days, William Shelley (1816–1819), Clara Everina Shelley (1817–1818), and Percy Florence Shelley (1819–1889); and he declared himself the father of Elena Adelaide Shelley (1818–1820), who may have been illegitimate or adopted. Percy Florence Shelley became the third baronet in 1844 after Sir Timothy's death. Shelley was a political radical influenced by Rousseau, Paine, Godwin, Wollstonecraft, and Leigh Hunt; he advocated Catholic emancipation, republicanism, parliamentary reform, extension of the franchise, freedom of speech and peaceful assembly, an end to aristocratic and clerical privilege, and a more equal distribution of income and wealth. His published works often reflected more moderate views than his private beliefs due to the risk of prosecution for seditious libel and his desire not to alienate moderate allies, though his political writings and activism led to government surveillance. His most influential political work after death was the poem Queen Mab, which included extensive political notes and went through 14 official and pirated editions by 1845, becoming popular in Owenist and Chartist circles; his longest political essay, A Philosophical View of Reform, was written in 1820 but not published until 1920. Shelley's advocacy of nonviolent resistance stemmed from his reflections on the French Revolution and the rise of Napoleon, and his belief that violent protest would lead to military despotism; although he sympathized with Irish independence supporters like Peter Finnerty and Robert Emmet, he did not support violent rebellion, as stated in his 1812 pamphlet An Address, to the Irish People: "I do not wish to see things changed now, because it cannot be done without violence, and we may assure ourselves that none of us are fit for any change, however good, if we condescend to employ force in a cause we think right." In A Philosophical View of Reform, he conceded that force might be justified in extreme circumstances: "The last resort of resistance is undoubtably [sic] insurrection. The right of insurrection is derived from the employment of armed force to counteract the will of the nation." He supported the 1820 armed rebellion in Spain and the 1821 Greek uprising against Ottoman rule. His poem "The Mask of Anarchy" (written in 1819, first published in 1832) is considered "perhaps the first modern statement of the principle of nonviolent resistance"; Gandhi was familiar with it, and it is possible Shelley indirectly influenced Gandhi through Henry David Thoreau's Civil Disobedience. Shelley was an avowed atheist, influenced by Holbach's Le Système de la nature; his atheism was central to his political radicalism, as he viewed organized religion as tied to social oppression. The overt atheism in his works posed a risk of prosecution for religious libel; his early pamphlet The Necessity of Atheism was withdrawn after a priest's complaint, and Queen Mab was prosecuted twice by the Society for the Suppression of Vice in 1821. Many of his other works were edited before publication to avoid prosecution. Shelley advocated free love, drawing on Mary Wollstonecraft and William Godwin; in his notes to Queen Mab, he wrote: "A system could not well have been devised more studiously hostile to human happiness than marriage," arguing that children of unhappy marriages are raised in "a systematic school of ill-humour, violence and falsehood," and that the ideal of chastity outside marriage is "a monkish and evangelical superstition" leading to hypocrisy in prostitution and promiscuity. He believed that "sexual connection" should be free among those who love each other and last only as long as their mutual love, and that love should be free from obedience, jealousy, and fear; he denied that free love would lead to promiscuity or disruption of stable relationships, asserting that love-based relationships would be long-lasting and marked by generosity and self-devotion. When Shelley's friend T. J. Hogg made an unwanted sexual advance to Harriet, Shelley forgave him and assured him he was not jealous; it is likely that Shelley encouraged Hogg and his second wife Mary to have a sexual relationship. In early March 1812, Shelley adopted a vegetable diet and maintained it with occasional lapses for the rest of his life; his vegetarianism was influenced by ancient authors such as Hesiod, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Ovid, and Plutarch, and more directly by John Frank Newton, author of The Return to Nature, or, A Defence of the Vegetable Regimen (1811). He wrote two essays on vegetarianism: A Vindication of Natural Diet (1813) and "On the Vegetable System of Diet" (written c. 1813–1815, first published in 1929). Michael Owen Jones argues that Shelley's advocacy of vegetarianism was strikingly modern, emphasizing health benefits, animal suffering, inefficient land use in animal husbandry, and economic inequality in animal food production. Shelley's life and works inspired the founding of the Vegetarian Society in England (1847) and directly influenced George Bernard Shaw's vegetarianism. His work was not widely read during his lifetime outside a small circle of friends, poets, and critics; most of his poetry, drama, and fiction were published in editions of 250 copies that sold poorly. Only The Cenci received an authorized second edition while Shelley was alive, unlike Byron's The Corsair (1814), which sold out its first edition of 10,000 copies in one day. Initial reception in mainstream periodicals (except the liberal Examiner) was generally unfavourable, with reviewers often launching personal attacks on his private life and views, even acknowledging his poetic imagery and expression; Hazlitt described his poetry as "a passionate dream, a straining after impossibilities, a record of fond conjectures, a confused embodying of vague abstraction." Shelley's poetry gained wider appeal in radical and reformist circles, with Queen Mab becoming popular among Owenists and Chartists, and Revolt of Islam influencing poets like Thomas Hood, Thomas Cooper, and William Morris. His mainstream following did not develop until a generation after his death; Bieri argues that editions published in 1824 and 1839 were edited by Mary Shelley to highlight his lyrical gifts and downplay his radical ideas. Matthew Arnold famously described Shelley as a "beautiful and ineffectual angel." Shelley influenced major poets in later decades, including Robert Browning, Algernon Swinburne, Thomas Hardy, and William Butler Yeats; Shelley-like characters appear in works such as Scythrop in Thomas Love Peacock's Nightmare Abbey, Ladislaw in George Eliot's Middlemarch, and Angel Clare in Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles. Twentieth-century critics such as Eliot, Leavis, Allen Tate, and Auden criticized Shelley's poetry for deficiencies in style, "repellent" ideas, and immaturity of intellect and sensibility; however, his critical reputation began to rise in the 1960s as critics highlighted his debt to Spenser and Milton, his mastery of genres and verse forms, and the complex interplay of sceptical, idealist, and materialist ideas. Harold Bloom described him as "a superb craftsman, a lyric poet without rival, and surely one of the most advanced sceptical intellects ever to write a poem," and Donald H. Reiman stated that "Shelley belongs to the great tradition of Western writers that includes Dante, Shakespeare and Milton." At the time of his death, many of his works were unfinished, unpublished, or published in expurgated versions with errors. Since the 1980s, various projects have aimed to establish reliable editions of his manuscripts and works. Among the most notable is the rediscovery in 2006 of Shelley's long-lost "Poetical Essay on the Existing State of Things" (1811), which was made available online by the Bodleian Library in Oxford. Charles E. Robinson argues that Shelley made a significant contribution to Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein and that he should be considered her collaborator; Charlotte Gordon and others dispute this. Fiona Sampson notes that Percy's corrections in the Frankenstein notebooks at the Bodleian Library have been cited as evidence of co-authorship, but upon examination, she found that Percy's role was minimal, like that of a modern line editor. The Shelley Society was founded in London in 1885 by Frederick James Furnivall, with branches later established in provincial Britain and abroad, including in Australia, New Zealand, and the United States; its lectures, publications, and publicity helped popularize Shelley and shaped scholarly discussions on English literature. The society ceased regular operations in the early 20th century. The Keats–Shelley Memorial Association, founded in 1903, supports the Keats–Shelley Memorial House in Rome, a museum and library dedicated to Romantic writers with strong Italian connections; it also maintains Percy Bysshe Shelley's grave in the non-Catholic Cemetery at Testaccio. The association publishes the scholarly Keats–Shelley Review and runs the annual Keats–Shelley and Young Romantics Writing Prizes and the Keats–Shelley Fellowship.
